articles.title_orig: Stock futures edge lower after markets slide amid Nvidia woes: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures edge lower after markets slide amid Nvidia woes: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures fell early Friday after major indexes declined and Nvidia shares fell in regular trading, following the exit of the scandal-hit chipmaker's founder and CEO Jensen Huang.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were down 0.09%, while S&P 500 futures were down 0.14%. Nasdaq-100 futures fell 0.36%.
The action comes after the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 dropped about 0.4% each in regular trading. The Dow slid almost 190 points, or 0.4%. Nvidia's 4.3% decline dragged down the three major averages, even as the chip stock ended the session off its lows.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from his post at the chip company following reported extramarital affairs , including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.
Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress , who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.
A jump in oil prices also kept stocks under pressure Thursday, with Brent crude rising more than 3% on the day to settle at $95.82 a barrel. Oil climbed after President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post , "We don't need a deal with Iran." The comment raised concerns that the U.S.-Iran war could drag on further.
Another market catalyst awaits on Friday in the form of October's producer price index reading, a measure of wholesale inflation. Economists polled by Dow Jones see headline PPI rising 0.4% on the month and 6.6% from 12 months earlier.
Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages are heading for weekly advances. The Nasdaq is up 3.2%, while the S&P 500 is on pace for a 2.9% advance. The Dow is poised for a nearly 2% jump. All three indexes are heading for their best weekly performances since early August.
Asia-Pacific markets were mostly lower, with South Korea's Kospi down 0.98% and closing at 5,290.53.
China's CSI 300 slipped 0.68% to 4,016.29, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.6% lower in its final hour of trade. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 dropped 0.71% to end the day at 9,082.2.
The exception was Japan's Nikkei 225 , which was up 0.53%, ending at 61,142.35.
Microsoft shares were 3% lower in premarket trade at 4:35 a.m. ET, as the company's engineers continued to grapple with server issues that caused a widespread outage of its Outlook service, disrupting businesses, governments and the general public around the world.
Outlook was inaccessible via app or browser throughout the Asian business day and into Europe's morning, with related services also impacted. Connectivity issues began around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday, hitting hundreds of thousands of U.S. Microsoft users.
The company said at 4:14 a.m. ET on Friday that it was seeing "early signs of stabilization" but that service would be "variable," and it was working to preserve mail delayed during the recovery process. It added it was not aware if "malicious activity" was the cause of the incident.
Shares of Richemont are on track for their worst day since July 2023, even after the luxury conglomerate posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Friday.
Swiss-listed shares were down 6.8% in morning trading.
Sales rose 13% at constant exchange rates in the quarter ended September, while its important jewellery business, which includes Cartier and Van Cleef, grew 14%.
Results exceeded expectations; however, they marked a slowdown from the previous quarter, when total sales grew by 20% and jewellery grew by 24%.
The luxury sector has seen a prolonged slump amid higher pricing and overall softer demand, especially in China. Richemont said sales in mainland China were down about 3% in the first half of the fiscal year.
Luxury peers LVMH , Gucci-owner Kering and Hermes all traded lower in morning trading Friday.
Nvidia shares were slightly higher in premarket trading on Friday as investors navigate the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of at least two affairs.
It follows a wild day for the stock on Thursday, which dropped sharply before recovering to close just over 4% lower.
Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. He was already under scrutiny following an investigation by the board into his relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Read the full story here .
Treasury yields edged higher on Friday as investor expectations for a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve gathered strength.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 2 basis points to 5.1271%.
Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a near certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a 25 basis points hike now stand at almost 87%, with the chance of a 50 basis point increase at around 13%.
Shares of Richemont were 7.2% lower by 8:50 a.m. in London (3:50 a.m. ET), after the Swiss luxury giant released its fiscal first-half earnings on Friday morning.
In the six months to September, the company said sales jumped 16% year-on-year to 12.3 billion euros ($13.6 billion), slightly beating an analyst consensus estimate compiled by LSEG.
Operating profit surged 33% to 3.1 billion euros, while earnings per share rose to 4.29 euros from 3.08 euros in the same period a year earlier.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 0.2% in early trading on Friday, with most sectors and all major regional bourses in negative territory.
The Stoxx 600 Technology index fell 0.6% shortly after the opening bell, putting it on track for its second consecutive day of losses.
Chip stocks extended the sell-off that began Thursday ahead of Jensen Huang abdicating his position as Nvidia CEO. Dutch semiconductor equipment makers ASMI and ASML lost around 1.5% in early dealmaking, while Be Semiconductor was 1.1% lower and shares of Germany's Infineon shed 1.8%.
Asia-Pacific markets closed mostly lower Friday, capping off a week dominated by the Nvidia shakeup.
South Korea's Kospi fell 0.98% to close at 5,290.53, while the small-cap Kosdaq was up 0.45% at 699.66.
China's CSI 300 fell 0.68% to 4,016.29, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.6% lower in its final hour of trade.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 dropped 0.71% to end the day at 9,082.2
The exception was Japan's Nikkei 225 , which gained 0.53%, ending at 61,142.35, while the broader Topix rose 0.11% to 3,941.57.
Shares of Japanese sportswear giant Asics tumbled 14.3% on Friday, after the company's earnings disappointed investors.
Revenue for the firm's fiscal third quarter came in at 270.67 billion Japanese yen ($1.69 billion), below an analyst consensus of 279.6 billion yen compiled by LSEG. Operating profit hit 55.1 billion yen, representing a year-on-year rise of 18.4% but falling short of analyst estimates.
Friday's share move was the biggest one-day drop in Asics' share price since Aug. 2024.
A flash poll of members of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council and Financial Advisor 100 on Thursday showed 18 respondents are planning to hold their Nvidia allocations steady in client portfolios.
Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama reportedly said that Tokyo will continue to work with the U.S. to take appropriate action after the yen crossed 160 against the dollar on Thursday.
Katayama said Friday that "We're currently seeing sharp, one-sided moves in the foreign exchange market."

Jensen Huang, the billionaire co-founder of tech firm Nvidia, resigned as CEO after allegations of extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy rocked his company.
The 63-year-old’s departure comes in the wake of a scandal that has wiped an estimated $500 billion off the chipmaker’s market value , with share prices plunging 12 percent to start Thursday. However, they have rebounded some ad were down 5 percent by midday.
One of the world’s richest men, Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, which is now at the heart of the AI revolution. He is the company’s fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61 percent, and will exit the Nvidia board with immediate effect, the company announced Thursday.
“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” Nvidia said in a statement.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who is close to Huang , suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace him.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump posted Thursday on Truth Social. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”
When the board announced Huang’s resignation early Thursday it also stated that Colette Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, would serve as interim CEO.
“The Board, Estaff (executive staff) and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period,” Kress wrote in a memo to employees, adding the company will host a meeting on November 18.
Huang’s problems began when The New York Times reported he had had an affair with former Megaspeed director Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence has said facilitated shipments of Nvidia’s microchips to Chinese firms as part of a foreign intelligence operation.
The newspaper subsequently alleged that the executive had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell , his company’s vice president of healthcare, who is also married.
After the first of the infidelities was disclosed, the executive sent a memo to Nvidia employees Sunday admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife of 40 years , Lori Huang, and said he was “deeply sorry” for the hurt he had case without going into details. Nvidia’s board responded by launching an internal investigation .
China meanwhile denied the espionage claims, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
Huang’s exit creates a leadership vacuum at the $4 trillion chipmaker, that is the driving force behind the global AI boom and at the heart of the big tech arms race between the U.S. and China .
For years, Nvidia was best known to video gamers for helping produce top-tier graphics. But its chips' ability to perform many calculations at once has made them a strategic prize in the US-China race to dominate AI technology. It also made Nvidia the world's most valuable company.
The success turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who would ask him to sign books, posters and even their bodies.
Prior to the announcement, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, an expert on corporate governance at Yale School of Management, told NBC News the scandal meant Huang had “lost his legitimacy to lead internally in the eyes of the company, and he’s lost his external credibility in the eyes of key constituents, including customers.”
Before the resignation, fellow tech boss Elon Musk said it would be “an honor” to hire Huang, the pair having previously worked together on Tesla, xAI and space-based data center projects.
The world’s richest man recently said of Huang, “old friends are the best friends,” adding: “Jensen rocks.”
It is not yet clear whether Huang’s extramarital affairs will end his marriage. Forbes has estimated Lori Huang could receive a windfall of at least $75 billion if the couple does divorce, putting her in an exclusive tech billionaire ex-wives’ club that also includes Melinda French Gates and MacKenzie Scott.
The scandal has also reverberated in Washington, D.C., with reports that Trump was warned about Huang’s compromised position by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in May when the executive joined their visit to Beijing.
Earlier this week, Trump said he had “absolutely no idea” that the first reported affair was with a suspected Chinese spy.
“I think ​he's an honorable guy," Trump said, adding ​that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country.”
Republican leaders of three House committees have meanwhile called for Huang to deliver closed-door testimony on his interactions with the alleged intelligence asset. Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have written to Trump’s commerce secretary Howard Lutnick to demand that all company records relating to Nvidia’s dealings with China be preserved.
Nvidia has started a search for a new permanent CEO and said it had full confidence in Kress, the interim leader.
“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia’s board of directors.
“The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
Rhian Lubin contributed to this report from New York

articles.title_orig: Global Microsoft outage leaves millions without access to Outlook email, Teams and other tools
articles.title_zh: Global Microsoft outage leaves millions without access to Outlook email, Teams and other tools
articles.content_orig:
• Hours-long outage: A Microsoft outage that began over 12 hours ago has left millions around the world without access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life. Banks, governments and courts in multiple countries are affected.
• No quick fix: The tech giant is struggling to fix the problem , which it said was not caused by a cybersecurity breach .
• Global disruption: Outage reports “reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour,” according to Downdetector. In the US, city governments across the country reported widespread email disruptions. In the UK, a disruption to the National Health Service email system is expected to prevent some patients from getting their drug prescriptions.
Microsoft said that it would extend its email timeout window to 48 hours “to help protect delayed messages while service recovery continues,” according to an update posted at around 4:15 a.m. ET Friday.
The email timeout window is the maximum amount of time that a mail server or email client such as Outlook will spend waiting to receive an email before returning an error.
Microsoft said recovery efforts are ongoing and that it’s seeing “early signs of stabilization,” though service capacity has not returned to normal.
Memes and jokes abounded online as the global outage of Microsoft’s Outlook emails and Teams meeting platform crossed the 12-hour mark.
One joke that spread on Threads , X and LinkedIn was the rebrand of Microsoft365 to Microsoft364 – memorializing the one day of the year that the software company went dark.
Others reveled at not needing to respond to constant emails and notifications for at least one day.
Another account wrote : “Outlook is down. Your email does not find me well. It does not find me at all.”
Others on Reddit said they panicked and thought they were laid off when they could not access their work emails.
At first, Microsoft said the connection issues were happening “in the Americas,” but over time it became clear the troubles were global.
Microsoft’s outage reports “reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour,” according to Downdetector, a website that tracks cyber outages.
Here’s where we’ve seen reports of outages:
CNN’s Brian Stelter, Hilary Whiteman and Junko Ogura contributed to this report.
A Microsoft outage causing disruptions to the email system of the UK’s National Health Service is expected to prevent some patients from getting their drug prescriptions Friday.
The outage “affects a pharmacy’s ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients,” a spokesperson for the National Pharmacy Association said in a Friday statement.
GPs are equivalent to family doctors in the US.
An NPA spokesperson told CNN in a separate phone call that, while many patients will get their medications, those with more complex prescriptions requiring a pharmacist to contact the prescribing doctor to check or query any details could experience delays.
The spokesperson added that Fridays are typically busy days at pharmacies.
“It’s just a massive pain. It will be slow today,” they said.
More than 12 hours after Microsoft first warned of a global outage affecting some of its most popular products, the company said it had “observed marginal success” in fixing the problem.
“We’re continuing to monitor activity across regions to evaluate server status and determine actions that can be taken to improve capacity,” Microsoft said in a statement posted on its Service Health Status page early Friday.
“At this point, we have observed marginal success,” the company wrote.
Around 30 minutes later, Microsoft posted another statement saying the company has seen “positive results for service stability and increased capacity as a result of our latest traffic optimization actions.”
Reiterating what it said earlier Thursday, Microsoft stated it was not aware of any malicious activity causing the outage but will continue to treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.”
The Microsoft global outage is ongoing after the US tech giant first reported problems with its email services on Thursday.
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use its Copilot AI chatbot, according to the company’s website.
Millions worldwide lost access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other essentials of modern office life as the disruption quickly spread .
The company reported “marginal success” in repairing the outage in its latest update, early Friday ET. A Microsoft executive confirmed the outage was not the result of a security breach.
As Europe woke on Friday, the outage remained widespread.
Here’s the latest if you’re just tuning in:
CNN’s Helen Regan, Hilary Whiteman, Karina Tsui, Kathleen Magramo and Ross Adkin contributed reporting.
Several airlines are reporting disruptions to their email support and communications due to the Microsoft outage, posting statements to customers on social media.
Indian budget carrier IndiGo said its “email support services are currently impacted, and we may not be able to receive your emails.” It directed customers to reach out via their website or mobile app.
Akasa Air, another low-cost Indian carrier, similarly said its “email support services are currently experiencing delays.”
And South African carrier CemAir said it was “experiencing some system disruptions due to the global Microsoft outage.”
None of the carriers reported flight disruptions.
Indian flag carrier Air India said it was “closely monitoring the ongoing Microsoft outage” and has rerouted emails. The airline said its flight operations “remain unaffected” and “there is currently no impact on any of our communication channels.”
“Consider this your cue to plan that getaway.”
The Microsoft outage comes at a time when Europe is pushing for greater tech sovereignty, aiming to run its own servers and reduce dependency on foreign providers.
Europe lacks the kind of mega tech companies that abound in the US, making it reliant on American firms for its digital services, but there is sentiment in Europe that it should become less reliant on the United States for its tech needs.
That sentiment has hardened during US President Donald Trump’s second term, when he has hit the continent with huge tariffs and threatened to take over the Danish territory of Greenland .
Earlier this year French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said that government officials will ditch Zoom and other US-owned video conferencing tools and begin using French-owned software. The decision is intended partly to reduce “dependencies on non-European actors,” Lecornu said.
“The internet in Europe is essentially a US construct, a US system. And Europe doesn’t really have a competitor to any of that,” Neil Shearing, group chief economist at Capital Economics, told CNN earlier this year.
On Friday, that question resurfaced as Microsoft’s outage stretched beyond 12 hours, disrupting countries across the globe .
“That tech sovereignty conversation, while it’s been mostly political, I bet it’s real sharp today,” technology journalist and founder of The Rip Current podcast Jacob Ward told CNN.
CNN’s Anna Cooban contributed reporting.
City governments across the United States have reported widespread email disruptions since Microsoft’s global outage began and have encouraged residents to call local offices and agencies if necessary.
The outages are affecting inbound and outbound email services at local government offices across major cities, including Miami Beach , Austin , and Jacksonville , though officials assured residents that emergency services were still active.
Baltimore County officials said on X that government staff could not send or receive emails and urged residents to contact relevant departments by phone.
In California, officials from the cities of Pasadena , Fremont , Burbank , and Santa Barbara also issued statements warning of downed email use.

articles.title_orig: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search
articles.title_zh: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia in scandal leaves the company without its visionary leader. It also leaves a major void for the AI industry, where Huang was kingmaker in inking deals to support the tech boom.
Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia became more than a chipmaker: It guaranteed deals for data centers, invested heavily in AI startups and even backed the companies that bought its products.
Huang put Nvidia at the core of AI financing, and the CEO himself championed some of the industry’s biggest deals. His departure puts a spotlight on whether the ecosystem he crafted could fracture — and whether that would spell trouble for the AI boom that has helped prop up the US stock market and become a driving force of economic growth.
“It’s hard to overstate his personal role in all of this,” said Neil Wilson, a strategist at investment bank Saxo.
“Huang was key in Nvidia being the backer of last resort across the AI ecosystem, really underpinning a lot of the financing and infrastructure guarantees,” he said.
Nvidia backstopped deals, like committing $105 billion in August for an OpenAI data center. The company has a major equity stake in the neocloud CoreWeave, emerging as an important financial backer and confidence booster. Nvidia is expected to take a $10 billion stake in Anthropic’s initial public offering.
Nvidia makes the graphics processing units that power AI models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. But the company has also been “the central bank of AI,” Jay Goldberg, senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, told CNN.
The company also functions like a venture capitalist, Goldberg noted, investing in companies to fuel their growth and help them get ahead in an industry that requires massive amounts of capital.
“Circular financing” has emerged as a term to describe Nvidia’s financial agreements, because the company is backing the companies that, in turn, buy its products. Goldberg said a more accurate term would be “very aggressive vendor financing.”
The company’s financial commitments in the AI boom have grown to the point that it had to address the associated risks in its latest quarterly earnings filing.
“Commitments, guarantees and other commercial arrangements expose us to financial, counterparty and execution risks and may not provide anticipated benefits,” Nvidia said in its most recent quarterly earnings report.
Huang’s sudden fall from grace puts that financing strategy in question. He resigned amid revelations extramarital affairs and a board investigation into whether he was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.”
Just three months ago, after committing the $105 billion for the OpenAI data center, Huang brought together six major financial institutions — Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR — to agree to treat Nvidia’s AI infrastructure as an asset class to write debt against, with aims of mobilizing over $500 billion for the AI boom.
“That was all driven by [Huang],” Goldberg said, adding that the deal isn’t finalized, and he expects it will come under additional review (and could even fall through).
Jensen Huang is living proof that AI’s rockstar CEOs are also a hidden risk
Nvidia’s central role in AI financing is directly related to the so-called neoclouds, or companies that rent out compute to power the boom.
Nvidia, as the primary provider of technology to power AI, has reaped massive profits in recent years. The company has used its cash to invest in neoclouds like CoreWeave and also provide backstops by guaranteeing to step in and provide revenue if they can’t sell all the compute capacity from Nvidia’s GPUs.
If Nvidia loses its savvy as an AI financier, it muddies the outlook for the neocloud industry, which relies on Nvidia as a bedrock to help issue those guarantees that help companies lock in more affordable interest rates.
In October, when CoreWeave’s bond yields spiked, the situation only calmed after Huang stepped in and expressed confidence in the company’s future. “I’m optimistic,” Huang told Bloomberg News on October 15. CoreWeave stock rallied 6% that day, snapping a three-day slide.
“This just raises the pressure on some of the smaller neoclouds’ ability to raise capital,” Goldberg said.
“When we lose Jensen, we lose a lot of the animating force that’s been driving the industry,” Goldberg said. “So, the world just feels a little bit smaller without him.”
Huang’s financing strategy not only supports the growth of the AI boom, but effectively secured Nvidia’s status as the axis on which everything was connected.
The AI industry’s existing long-term agreements mean the near-term outlook likely stays the same, Goldberg said. But, over time, Nvidia’s ability to deploy the same creative financing strategies could become less certain and potentially slow the industry’s expansion.
While Nvidia announced Thursday that Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, would be interim CEO, potentially reassuring investors, replacing Huang’s dealmaking expertise will be a much bigger challenge.
“He was not only the chief technology architect … but he was also the capital allocator,” Ted Mortonson, tech strategist at Baird, told CNN.
“With him leaving, it leaves a huge void,” Mortonson said.
Nvidia also faces competition for its role as the core provider of compute, with other semiconductor companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom already building alternatives to the company’s GPUs.
Uncertainty over Nvidia’s role could put pressure on other tech companies, or the hyperscalers like Alphabet and Amazon, to step up as the capital allocator Nvidia has been. But it remains to be seen who can champion the industry and execute dealmaking like Huang.
Huang’s dual role as the man who understood the tech and the dealmaker who understood the financing was a unique combination that contributed to his star-status role, Mortonson said.
Huang gave Nvidia the clout and ability to dictate terms on pricing and deals, analysts said. Without Huang, that ability becomes less apparent.
“Jensen’s successor will not have the same latitude or deference to pursue circular deals and pursue aggressive sales tactics,” Mike O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, told CNN in an email.
“There’s the quantifiable and the unquantifiable,” said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, a fund focused on founder-led companies.
“There are things you can’t put in a spreadsheet, right?,” Monaghan said. “He has that aura, plus all of that engineering knowledge, plus all of the 33 years of building all this stuff. You just can’t replace that.”
“Jensen knew where to put his own capital to help grow the ecosystem, and that walks out the door with him,” Monaghan said.
Demand for AI is robust. Anthropic’s revenue in the third quarter soared more than 1,000% year-over-year, a sign that people are adopting and paying for AI. Companies are likely to keep investing in infrastructure to meet the demand. But investors ultimately want to see those investment turn into profits, or may begin to question whether the massive spending is justified.
Huang’s departure shakes the foundation of the sprawling web of financing that has come to define the AI economy. A slowdown in dealmaking could exacerbate cost pressures, spell trouble for smaller companies and create added headwinds that could hamper the AI trade.
“The risk is less about chip demand than about the money,” David Rosenberg, president and founder at Rosenberg Research, wrote in a note. “Nvidia’s stakes, guarantees and backstops are what tie the AI trade together, so the weakest links are the borrowers who depend on Nvidia’s support.”

articles.title_orig: Nvidia without Jensen Huang. What lies ahead for Asian chipmakers?
articles.title_zh: Nvidia without Jensen Huang. What lies ahead for Asian chipmakers?
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's leadership shake-up is unlikely to cause immediate disruption for major Asian semiconductor suppliers, such as Samsung Electronics and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., but Jensen Huang's departure has raised questions about the company's longer-term product strategy and supply chain relationships.
The bigger issue for investors and suppliers is whether Nvidia can maintain the pace of innovation and close ties with key partners that Huang helped drive as the company built its dominance in artificial intelligence chips.
In a Friday research note, Nam Dae-jong and Kim Yeon-mi, analysts at South Korean brokerage Daol Investment & Securities, said Huang's departure was unlikely to affect the semiconductor industry's near-term outlook.
However, they flagged uncertainty over Nvidia's medium- to long-term product roadmap, including how its new leadership would coordinate with partners across the AI ecosystem.
For chipmakers in Asia, one key question is whether Nvidia's relationships with its manufacturing partners could change under new leadership.
Nam and Kim expect Nvidia's foundry relationship with TSMC to remain unchanged, given the companies' established partnership.
They also expect Nvidia's relationship with Samsung's foundry business to continue, citing growing cooperation between the companies, including manufacturing involving Samsung's 4-nanometer process and work on next-generation high-bandwidth memory technology.
The analysts said custom AI chips, or application-specific integrated circuits, or ASICs, are emerging as alternatives to Nvidia's graphic processing units and could accelerate diversification in the AI chip market.
However, they cautioned against interpreting growing competition as a sign of weakening demand for memory semiconductors, particularly high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.
Still, uncertainty remains over Nvidia's longer-term product roadmap, given Huang's central role in shaping the company's business strategy and allocating resources.
SK Hynix, another key supplier to Nvidia, reversed earlier gains to close 3.03% lower on Friday.
In a research note earlier in the day, Shinhan Securities said investors had initially looked past concerns over Nvidia's leadership change and focused instead on the broader outlook for the AI industry.
South Korea's Kospi also reversed earlier gains Friday. In a research note, iM Securities said the impact of Nvidia's leadership change on the broader semiconductor sector appeared limited, pointing to gains in AMD and Broadcom shares in the previous U.S. session and continued investment demand for AI companies.
ASUS Co-CEO S.Y. Hsu told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " that Nvidia's leadership change was unlikely to alter its competitive advantages in the near term, though the company would monitor any impact on product quality, service costs and deliveries.
"I think Nvidia's product and the total AI ecosystem, the advantage will not change overnight," Hsu said.
ASUS, which works with Nvidia across graphics cards and AI servers, has yet to interact with interim CEO Colette Kress, Hsu said, adding that the company was seeking a meeting to better understand any potential strategic changes.
Over the longer term, Hsu said Huang had played a key role in helping Nvidia and its partners accelerate innovation, and that he would be watching to see whether the company could maintain that pace without him.

articles.title_orig: Lutnick should have prevented the diversion of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, critics charge
articles.title_zh: Lutnick should have prevented the diversion of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, critics charge
articles.content_orig:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Nvidia's ousted CEO Jensen Huang contributed to the federal agency's lack of oversight over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS has learned.
Before President Trump nominated Lutnick to lead the Commerce Department, Lutnick was the chairman and CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a New York investment bank which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time.
Lutnick developed a warm relationship with Huang, who resigned Thursday as reports of a growing number of affairs caused new uncertainty about the world's dominant AI chipmaker. One of Huang's alleged relationships was with Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen Huang), who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy. She ran Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that became one of Nvidia's biggest customers for AI chips and is suspected of illegally shipping Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to Chinese entities, circumventing a U.S. ban.
As commerce secretary, Lutnick took the helm of an agency responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals.
One way the Commerce Department keeps this information and technology out of the hands of China and other adversaries is by putting foreign companies and individuals on its Entity List . This restricts their ability to access U.S. technology products, and inclusion on the list means that the department believes there's a risk that the entity is involved in activities that are contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.
In 2024, under the Biden administration, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security launched an investigation into Nvidia's chip sales to Megaspeed to determine whether they were being redirected to China. But according to The New York Times , the probe was abruptly transferred to the Department of Justice. The Justice Department would not comment about the investigation.
The Commerce Department has not added a company to the Entity List since October 2025.
Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over the Commerce Department's failure to place Megaspeed on the Entity List, Axios reported.
Chris McGuire, an expert on China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said, "The real scandal here is the lack of enforcement of export controls."
He added that the Commerce Department had known for as long as a year that Megaspeed was being run by a woman who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy, "and they did nothing." The New York Times reported that about a year ago, President Trump was briefed on intelligence that suggested that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset and that she had grown close to Jensen Huang.
"Either Lutnick doesn't know how to do his job or he is protecting Huang," McGuire said.
The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.
On Thursday, after Jensen Huang's resignation became public, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, called on Lutnick and his deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, to "explain why they have not closed export control loopholes." Kessler is the undersecretary who led the Commerce Department's probe into Megaspeed.
Warren urged the two to "act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military." In March, Warren wrote to Lutnick to demand the "immediate pausing" of all export licenses of Nvidia chips destined for China.
Questions about Lutnick's own relationship with Chinese state companies have further complicated the ongoing Nvidia crisis.
A financial services firm Lutnick ran, BGC Group, had a 33% stake in a joint venture with China Credit Trust, a Chinese state-owned company whose largest shareholder is the China People's Insurance Company, another state enterprise.
Another firm he ran, Cantor Fitzgerald, is still overseen by his two eldest sons. That firm helped several Chinese companies go public in the U.S. Cantor Fitzgerald was also a key investor in Satellogic, a satellite company that is under contract with a Chinese data science company, Zhong Ke Guang Qi Space, until 2033.
His close China ties emerged as a topic at his Senate confirmation hearing last year. Senators questioned whether he could be unduly influenced by Chinese officials, and how he would safeguard U.S. technology.
Sen. Maria Cantwell, a Democrat from Washington state, grilled Lutnick on potential conflicts of interest with respect to his investments in Chinese companies, and Cantor Fitzgerald's financial interest in Tether, a cryptocurrency company with a large footprint in China.
Other senators asked about how he would safeguard U.S. technology from the Chinese Communist Party.
"How will you address different threats that we see coming from the CCP within these information and technology markets?" asked GOP Sen. Deb Fischer, of Nebraska.
Lutnick promised to be vigilant against threats from China.
"I take a very jaundiced view of China," he said in response to Fischer. "I think they only care about themselves and seek harm to us, and so we need to protect ourselves."
Before he was sworn in as commerce secretary in February 2025, Lutnick resigned from all of his corporate leadership posts, transferring his business empire to his children.
Since his tenure as commerce secretary began, Lutnick and his family's net worth doubled to $7.3 billion, thanks to his indirect stake in Tether, according to Forbes , which valued his holding in Tether at $5.4 billion. The stake, worth $1.7 billion in early 2025, has more than tripled in value.
"Can we be confident that he is looking out for the public interest?" asked Kathleen Clark, a law professor and expert on government ethics at Washington University in St. Louis. "What's going on with him raises a lot of red flags."
Lutnick's friendship with Jensen Huang may also be problematic, Clark told CBS News.
Huang met Lutnick soon after Lutnick began his term as commerce secretary, Huang told podcaster Joe Rogan last year.
"He started our conversation with, 'Jensen, this is Secretary Lutnick,'" said Huang. "'I just want to let you know that you're a national treasure. Nvidia is a national treasure. And whenever you need access to the president, the administration, you call us.'"
Huang added that every time he called the commerce secretary's office, "if I want to get something off my chest, express some concern, they're always available."
Huang also visited with President Trump. He attended a $1 million-per-person dinner at Mar-a-Lago in April 2025. At that time, Huang tried to convince Mr. Trump to lift restrictions on the company's less advanced H20 chip sales to China, according to The New York Times . Less than three months later, in July 2025, Mr. Trump lifted the restrictions. Nvidia's most advanced chip, the Blackwell, still cannot be sold directly to China.
In July 2025, Lutnick posted a photo to Instagram showing Huang in his trademark black leather jacket standing in the Oval Office next to Mr. Trump, who was seated at his desk. Lutnick is also in the photo along with other visitors.
"Great to meet in the Oval Office with Jensen Huang on the very day Nvidia crossed $4 trillion in market cap," the post said.

articles.title_zh: Calls for crackdown on China chip exports – as it happened

US House Speaker Mike Johnson has said ⁠there is a ​growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang .
Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US ⁠authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government. The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.
In the last week, representatives from both sides of the aisle have called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips; chips that could underpin China’s surging AI development.
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are ⁠widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US ​has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips ‌because it wants its own companies to stay ahead in the race.
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told ‌reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“
Congressional Republicans are keen to attach ​new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense authorisation bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity.
This live blog is now closed – but if you’d like to read more on Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia, our latest report is here .
Colette Kress – Nvidia’s interim CEO – was one of the few executives at the company willing to check Jensen Huang’s enormous, often risky ambitions, Reuters has reported, citing two sources familiar with the matter.
Kress ⁠and her staff clashed with Huang and the company’s sales team over the massive financing deals that fed into what some Wall Street critics deemed a circular AI economy, including investments in OpenAI ​and AI infrastructure companies such as Lambda, according to one of the people familiar with ‌the matter.
A proposed $250bn plan to support an OpenAI ‌data center project in Ohio was ultimately pared to $120bn.
“I think it’s unlikely anyone but Jensen is going to invest in his own customers as aggressively,” said a third source, a venture capital investor. ‌
Kress served as an important counterweight to Huang, whose ⁠success afforded him great latitude on key decisions, the sources said.
“Colette is a pragmatist,” a fourth source told Reuters. She can project calm and help stabilize markets while the search is ongoing, the person said, adding that Kress had been on recent calls to reassure customers and suppliers as the tumult inside the company unfolded.
Under her leadership, Nvidia is likely to “approach DC more like other tech companies do, by trying to build capital and make friends,” instead of picking “a fight over export controls” the way it did under Huang’s leadership, ‌the person said.
Jensen Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs, with his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with the former Nvidia chief for 25,000 yuan, while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they saw as the swift resignation of the former Nvidia CEO, and mourned the sudden end of his three decades at the top of the company.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m views overnight on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.
Meanwhile, Chinese AI companies are reportedly trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters .
Nvidia’s advanced chips have been at the centre of the US-China technology rivalry, with Washington restricting their exports to China over national security concerns.
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick will testify before Congress on the Nvidia scandal.
US lawmakers have called for clarity on what the Donald Trump’s administration knew about Nvidia chief Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman accused of spying for China.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.
Lutnick has come under scrutiny as the commerce department was mandated to review companies for national security risks before the Trump administration allowed Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.
Senate banking committee chair Tim Scott requested that Lutnick testify “for a public hearing regarding recent public reports about Nvidia and the Department of Commerce’s role that raises national security concerns”.
Scott has also requested Jensen Huang testify before the committee.
Malaysia’s government has said it is investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.
On Thursday Nvidia boss Jensen Huang resigned over an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang – an alleged Chinese spy and former top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based datacentre company.
Megaspeed is under scrutiny for allegedly steering Nvidia AI chips to China despite US export rules designed to slow the development of Beijing’s artificial intelligence sector.
Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) said is it investigating whether a local subsidiary of Megaspeed reexported any chips brought into the country to other locations.
MITI said it was also working “closely” with authorities in Singapore and the United States “and is considering further measures to strengthen controls where necessary”.
Republican Senator Jim Banks has said that for the last two years, US lawmakers have been pushing to stop America’s “high-end computer chips from being exported to China.”
Banks said he hoped that Jensen Huang would come and testify before Congress.

In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration ‌had held off from adding China’s AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the trade blacklist.

articles.title_orig: After meeting Putin, U.S. envoys say Europe to join talks on ending Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: After meeting Putin, U.S. envoys say Europe to join talks on ending Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of news from two days of talks on Tuesday, November 10 and Wednesday, November 11:
This blog covering the trilateral Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi has now closed. Thank you for reading.
Join us on Thursday for fresh coverage as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner separatelymeet with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte offered a characteristically upbeat appraisal of the talks in Abu Dhabi and the prospect of cracks emerging between European NATO members, Ukraine and Donald Trump's administration in the US.
"I was in touch with the NATO team present in Abu Dhabi in the last two days," he told reporters while on a visit to Norway. "What I am getting from those calls is that the US, Ukraine and Europe really being completely aligned and united."
However, he cautioned that "clearly we have to see that the Russian side is willing to play ball."
After more than a decade as prime minister of the Netherlands, Rutte has taken on the unenviable job of trying to keep NATO aligned and united more generally during Donald Trump's second term . He stepped into the role a matter of weeks before the 2024 presidential election in the US.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy landed in Dublin on Wednesday evening, as he and his team head to the ninth European Political Community Summit.
He said both bilateral and multilateral meetings were planned amid his visit to Ireland .
"I will take part in the opening plenary session of the EPC Summit. A meeting on diplomatic efforts with the American negotiating team — Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner — is also planned," he said on social media.
Kushner and Witkoff are first expected to head to Moscow from Abu Dhabi, before moving on to Dublin on Thursday.
The European Political Community is an intergovernmental forum for strategic discussions about the future of Europe. It was set up in 2022, in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The group's ninth summit is scheduled to start early on Thursday morning and to continue until roughly the end of the working day. Hosts Ireland are also the current holders of the EU's rotating presidency.
Kyrylo Budanov described the talks in Abu Dhabi as "tough."
"Ukraine's position remains unchanged," Volodymyr Zelenskyy's chief of staff said on Telegram.
"The war must be brought to a halt, and an effective security architecture must be established — on that ensures a lasting peace and makes any recurrence of Russian aggression impossible."
He said returning Ukrainian prisoners was a "specific focus" of the talks, seemingly a reference to the prisoner swap plans, saying "we have achieved a significant result in this regard."
Budanov also thanked US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff "for their professionalism, persistence, and efforts in seeking solutions," and thanked the UAE for hosting the talks and supporting the process.
Russia's ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died "suddenly" at the age of 66, the Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
Darchiev was quite new in the job, having been appointed in March 2025 shortly after Donald Trump's return to the White House. From 2021 to 2024, he was ambassador to Canada.
The ministry called Darchiev an "outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader and a kind colleague."
It did not provide further details on the death.
Considered a specialist in US relations, Darchiev headed the Russian Foreign Ministry's North America department between 2014 and 2020 before graduating to ambassadorial roles.
When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, he called the move a "necessary measure."
Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky is quoted by state media as saying Moscow saw no possibility of exchanging territory with Ukraine as part of any potential agreement.
State news agency TASS quoted him saying there was "no possibility whatsoever for such exchanges."
TASS and Interfax also both cited Medinsky as saying that Russia had decided to establish a "security zone" along its border with Ukraine following the incursion into Kursk.
"This zone is already quite substantial, it is expanding — and will continue to expand," he said.
The reported comments did not make clear where Medinsky considered the border or the so-called buffer zones to be, quite possibly by design. Russia already claims large chunks of what the international community considers to be Ukraine as parts of its territory following its invasion.
Yuri Ushakov, a foreign policy advisor to Vladimir Putin and part of the Russian negotiating team, on Wednesday described the talks in Abu Dhabi as substantive and very useful.
Moscow's delegation is led by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, an another aide to Putin.
But Ushakov is also involved, along with deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabko and Mikhail Galuzin, and General Staff officers Igor Kostyukov and Yuri Shigarlovsky on the military side.
German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius has said that following the talks in Abu Dhabi, talks between Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President Vladimir Putin could become more likely.
Asked at a Berlin press conference whether Merz would be ready to speak with Putin, Kornelius said that during the talks in Abu Dhabi negotiators from Europe, the US and Ukraine — but not Russia — had reached an "understanding on the broad outlines."
"This understanding will now be shared with the Russian president. And on that basis, talks may ensue," Kornelius said.
This follows intimations from both sides that the German and Russian leaders might be ready to engage directly.
Russian state news agency Tass cited the Kremlin as saying that Putin would be open to talks with EU leaders including Merz, echoing comments made earlier this year .
Merz, meanwhile, had said last Friday that if Putin were to travel to December's G20 summit in Miami as rumored, he would not rule out a meeting.
Rustem Umerov, currently the head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence service and also its chief negotiator at the talks, also issued a statement following the roughly two hours of trilateral negotiations on Wednesday.
The former defense minister said negotiators discussed "achieving peace and post-war reconstruction," adding that "the first steps towards this must be an end to the war and security guarantees for Ukraine."
Over these two days, the parties were able to state their positions directly, and significant differences remain between them," Umerov said on Telegram.
"There is still a lot of difficult work ahead, but there are opportunities to continue the negotiation process."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had received a report on the Abu Dhabi talks from his negotiating team in Abu Dhabi.
He hailed an "important humanitarian arrangement regarding preparations for a new exchange," seemingly a reference to prisoner exchange plans. Zelenskyy also said negotiators discussed "their views on guaranteeing security" for Ukraine, as well as "broader formats for further work involving the Europeans" going forward.
Currently in Copenhagen in Denmark, Zelenskyy said his team would meet US negotiators in Dublin on Thursday, after they head to Moscow. But he also called for more European representation going forward.
"Ukraine's priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace," Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
"We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy. It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war — that is Russia — so that Russia ends the war of its own making."
Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia praised "good momentum" after the two-day talks in Abu Dhabi.
"I think that we have a good momentum to bring the solution before the new year comes," Arakhamia said, adding that he hoped another session could be held "as soon as possible."

articles.title_orig: Column | Jensen Huang’s leather jackets are juvenile delinquent drag
articles.title_zh: Column | Jensen Huang’s leather jackets are juvenile delinquent drag
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: Featuring the good, the bad and the ugly, ‘Look of the Week’ is a regular series dedicated to unpacking the most talked about outfit of the last seven days.
When an image purportedly showing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in his first public appearance since reports of an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy surfaced online, it quickly went viral. Huang was sporting a different look than usual. Instead of his signature smooth motorcycle-style leather jacket, he wore a much more ostentatious, studded version that online commentators quickly identified as Hedi Slimane-era Saint Laurent, an eye-catching archival grail for a man under siege.
There’s only one problem. “Those images are fake,” a spokesperson for Nvidia said in an email.
The photo’s proliferation speaks to the growing impossibility of distinguishing real from fake as AI tools — like the ones Nvidia’s chips power — further permeate our personal algorithms. In theory, it would have been a great (and distracting) look: a very flashy stepping out for a very difficult moment in the AI mogul’s career. His admission to an affair has since punctured his public image and sent his company’s shares tumbling.
“First person in history to have negative aura wearing archive Hedi,” read one comment with over a thousand likes on a post featuring the images, referring to Slimane, the French designer who served as Saint Laurent’s’s creative director from 2012 to 2016 before taking the reins at Celine until 2024.
The images appear to be altered from a real image of Huang arriving at Seoul’s Gimpo International Airport in June. They were seemingly plausible in part because the jacket was a variation on Huang’s uniform. The AI leader is almost always seen in a slim-cut leather jacket. He has, he told CBS , close to 30 or 40 leather jackets. Like other tech leaders who have opted for uniforms in the mold of Steve Jobs’ Issey Miyake black turtlenecks, he cited the fact that wearing the same outfit makes it easier for him to focus his attention on bigger things (like building a technology quickly taking over huge swaths of the global economy).
“Black is the absence of choice,” he told CBS. “That’s one decision made, one less thing to deal with. For everybody else, they probably have to make 3 or 4 decisions. I took that off my plate. It’s fantastic.”
CNN’s Zoe Sottile explains the viral AI-generated photo in the midst of a very real crisis for Nvidia
Huang’s classic leather jacket is an edgier, more striking look than the slouchy t-shirts favored by Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman. It’s the favored garment of bikers everywhere, James Dean wannabes, and anyone trying to embody an ideal of timeless cool.
He occasionally wears variations, like a reptile-skin version he sported for a keynote speech at the 2026 Consumer Electronics Show. One of his pieces, a Tom Ford jacket touted as the “CEO’s Uniform” and the “Jensen Jacket,” was auctioned by Sotheby’s earlier this year, which described it as “a symbol of his leadership style embodying authenticity, ingenuity, persistence, courage and joy.” It sold for close to $1 million, roughly double the presale estimates.
Huang, who has been married to his college sweetheart since 1985, has admitted to having an affair, saying he “hurt his wife and children,” but hasn’t named the other person involved. US intelligence have concluded in a classified memo issued in May that a close associate of Huang’s Alice Huang (no relation) was a Chinese intelligence asset.
In interviews, he’s attributed his signature look to his wife Lori, who he told CBS buys his jackets for him.
“I’m happy that my wife and daughter dress me,” he said in an interview for HP’s tech podcast “The Moment” in 2023.

articles.title_orig: At America’s Expense, Chinese Influence is on the Rise in Thailand
articles.title_zh: At America’s Expense, Chinese Influence is on the Rise in Thailand
articles.content_orig:
Despite its longstanding security alliance with the United States, Thailand—like most ASEAN states—has traditionally hedged between Washington and Beijing, seeking to benefit from both without choosing sides. But President Donald Trump’s increasingly unpredictable foreign policy is complicating Bangkok’s delicate balancing act. As confidence in Washington erodes, Thailand appears to be gravitating toward Beijing, which Thai leaders increasingly regard as a more stable and predictable partner.
In April, for example, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow criticized the “unpredictability” of U.S. foreign policy, arguing that Washington’s actions were “forcing us to rethink some relationships,” while suggesting that China, despite its own coercive tendencies, was comparatively more predictable. In September, Sihasak warned that intensifying strategic competition was putting ASEAN’s economic relationships and unity under pressure. More recently, on October 12, Royal Thai Air Force Commander Seksan Khantha declared that “there is no such thing as neutrality, but we must maintain a balance,” adding that Thailand’s best approach was to “love them both.” Meanwhile, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has sought to preserve strong economic ties with Washington while expanding cooperation with Beijing. Taken together, these remarks suggest that Thailand remains committed to hedging, but growing doubts about American reliability are creating opportunities for China to expand its influence.
Beijing, for its part, is wasting little time capitalizing on Bangkok’s growing uncertainty about Washington. During Prime Minister Anutin’s July 16th visit to China, he met President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang, with both sides agreeing to significantly expand their strategic partnership. The visit produced 15 agreements covering trade, investment, artificial intelligence, space technology, nuclear fusion, and other sectors. Perhaps most significantly, Beijing and Bangkok agreed to establish a new “2+2” dialogue between their foreign and defense ministers, expand defense-industrial cooperation and military training, and accelerate construction of the China–Thailand high-speed railway. Xi also portrayed China as a “trustworthy and reliable strategic cooperative partner,” reinforcing Beijing’s efforts to present itself as a dependable alternative to Washington. China is likely to continue engaging with Thailand at Washington’s expense.
But Thailand’s growing tilt toward China is not simply about Trump, even if his policies have accelerated the trend. His reciprocal tariffs, in particular, have angered and frustrated Bangkok, which expected more favorable treatment from its longtime American ally. Thailand initially faced a proposed 36 percent reciprocal tariff, later reduced to 19 percent. Sihasak has explicitly criticized American unpredictability, including tariffs, and acknowledged that Thailand is reconsidering some relationships. Yet the U.S.-Thailand alliance has struggled to find a clear strategic purpose since the end of the Cold War, and successive Thai governments have increasingly questioned its relevance. More fundamentally, Bangkok simply does not view China as a threat in the same way Washington does, making closer cooperation with Beijing a far more attractive proposition than American policymakers might appreciate.
Going forward, the United States and Thailand will need to identify new areas of cooperation to reinvigorate their longstanding alliance and broader strategic partnership. Trump’s interest in securing critical minerals, for example, could offer one such opportunity, particularly as Washington seeks to diversify supply chains away from China. Other promising areas include defense technology, cybersecurity, maritime security, and joint responses to transnational threats. But Washington will also need to recognize that Bangkok has little interest in choosing sides between the United States and China. Ultimately, the future of the U.S.-Thai alliance may depend less on countering Beijing directly than on demonstrating that Washington remains an indispensable partner in its own right.
Derek Grossman is CGSP’s Non-Resident Fellow for the Asia-Pacific

SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.
Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.
You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.
Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.
The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.
SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy , pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.
So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.
"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description .
The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit .
The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.
Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.
There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.
So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page .

articles.title_orig: Russia loses almost half a million lives in war on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russia loses almost half a million lives in war on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Death records reveal losses since full-scale invasion that are unprecedented in Russia’s modern history
Postwar ‘security guarantees’ a key focus in upcoming Abu Dhabi talks, says Rubio
More than 400,000 Russians have been killed fighting in Ukraine since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion nearly five years ago, according to data leaked from the state statistics agency, Rosstat.
The information, obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacking collective Silent Crow, contains more than 11m death certificates, including details of the deceased’s age, place of residence and location of death.
It was later shared with the Guardian and a small group of other media outlets.
According to the data, 412,576 death certificates explicitly linked the fatalities to the war, either through official cause-of-death codes or written references to combat and military operations.
The figures underscore the staggering human toll of Russia’s war against Ukraine, with no end in sight despite a fresh round of peace talks scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi this week.
The two hacking groups announced the breach on 1 November and published the data over the weekend. Rosstat confirmed it had been hacked but denied that any sensitive information had been obtained.
The dataset offers an unprecedentedly detailed picture of Russia’s wartime losses, which Moscow has sought to conceal. The Russian authorities have not published a death toll since the early months of the invasion, and information about military casualties is treated as a state secret.
The Guardian could not independently verify the authenticity of the entire dataset. However, the figures are broadly consistent with other estimates of Russian losses. British intelligence in September estimated that about 500,000 Russian soldiers had been killed since the start of the invasion.
Separately, the independent Russian outlet Mediazona has identified by name nearly 286,000 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine, drawing on official records, social media obituaries and photographs of gravestones. The outlet estimates the true toll is closer to half a million.
“The data looks authentic, and it’s very rich,” said Janis Kluge, the head of the Russia and Eurasia division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs.
“This is the biggest leak of data when it comes to Russian casualties,” added Kluge, who has studied Russian war statistics extensively.
The dataset is likely to underestimate the true death toll. Some soldiers remain missing, while others have never been identified.
Kluge also pointed to a significant delay between deaths occurring and being entered into official records, which he said typically took about six months.
“We are probably at this time closer to 500,000 killed Russian soldiers than 400,000,” he said.
The figures also reveal the unequal burden of the war across Russia, with poorer and more remote regions sustaining disproportionately heavy losses.
In Buryatia, Tuva and Zabaykalsky Krai, three regions in eastern Russia, war-related fatalities accounted for about a third of all deaths among men aged 18 to 49 between the start of the invasion and mid-2024. In Moscow and St Petersburg, the equivalent figure was about 10%.
There was also a sharp rise in Russian battlefield deaths as the war dragged on, with some of the deadliest months coming in late 2024 and 2025.
Kluge, who has been analysing the data, said the number of soldiers killed in several months during that period exceeded 15,000, equivalent to roughly 500 a day.
after newsletter promotion
“In late 2024 and in 2025, you see that the numbers in many months are above 15,000 per month, and that’s higher than I think most estimates were,” Kluge said. “That’s 500 a day, above 500 a day. Certainly shocking.”
The scale of the losses is staggering by any measure and unprecedented in Russia’s modern history.
In less than five years, Russian military deaths in Ukraine are estimated to have exceeded the combined death toll from all Soviet and Russian wars between the end of the second world war and the start of the full-scale invasion more than eightfold. The figure also exceeds the number of US military personnel who died during the second world war.
Rather than push Moscow towards a settlement, the scale of the losses is likely to harden Vladimir Putin’s resolve, according to a person familiar with the Russian president’s thinking.
“Putin understands these numbers, and for him to now settle for anything less than everything he wants would feel like a betrayal of himself and the people,” the person said.
Senior Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for the first US-brokered peace talks between them in nine months.
Previous negotiations have made little progress towards ending the war, with Moscow demanding that Ukraine withdraw from the parts of the Donbas region it still controls.
Neither Putin nor his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, will attend the talks. Instead, both countries will send senior delegations, with Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also expected to take part.
In a post on X, Witkoff said the negotiations would focus on “post-war security arrangement, de-escalation” and humanitarian issues.
European governments have expressed concern that the talks could extend beyond Ukraine to broader questions of European security, including Moscow’s longstanding demands for a reduction of Nato’s military presence in countries bordering Russia.
France’s foreign minister said Paris would participate in the negotiations but the Kremlin subsequently denied that France would be represented.

articles.title_orig: Zelda Ocarina's ReDead Were Set To Be "Very, Very Scary" In The Remake, But Nintendo Decided To "Dial It Back"
articles.title_zh: Zelda Ocarina's ReDead Were Set To Be "Very, Very Scary" In The Remake, But Nintendo Decided To "Dial It Back"
articles.content_orig:
Ocarina of Time's Switch 2 remake isn't really a scary game, but there are still some enemies throughout this adventure that may give players a fright.
Perhaps the most notable are ReDead , the zombie-like creatures that are difficult to escape when they set their sights on Link. These return in the remake and apparently were even scarier at one point during development, until Nintendo decided to "dial it back".
Here's what producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi had to say about this during a recent interview with GameSpot :
"With this remake, the graphics are a lot improved, and so the ReDead–the sound, the graphics, and the movement–ended up being very, very scary. And the staff wanted to make this in service of making a good gameplay experience. But from our perspective, taking a step back, we felt like, let’s remember the experience that we don’t want to change, and taking that into consideration, maybe we’ve gone a step too far, so let’s dial it back."
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
So, the decision was made to ensure the experience was more in line with the original game. The final result is the ReDead are still somewhat scary, but not "very, very scary" to the point it changes the experience.

articles.title_orig: Federal Reserve to Forgo Rate Decision at October 2027 Meeting
articles.title_zh: Federal Reserve to Forgo Rate Decision at October 2027 Meeting
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve won't vote on a potential interest-rate change at its October 2027 meeting, a departure that is part of a broader initiative from Chairman Kevin Warsh aimed at reducing the central bank's market footprint.
According to an announcement Thursday, the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will set aside its Oct. 26-27 session for "the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues."
Warsh announced the move at his news conference after the FOMC met in October, though he did not specify which meeting would be affected.
In 2027, there will be seven voting meetings, with the October session set up as extra time for policy deliberation without a formal vote or post-meeting statement. The new calendar shows that the final meeting of the year will now take place in November. It had previously been set for December.
"Now, what's the reasoning behind this change? To me, it's quite straightforward," the chairman said in explaining his rationale. "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals."
"But it's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations—for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point," he said.
Warsh has been critical of the Fed's prior communications strategy, saying policymakers spent too much time providing guidance on policy moves that handcuffed them when it came time to make decisions.
Under typical practice, the Fed meets eight times a year, following with a vote on interest rates and then a news conference from the chair.
Since Warsh took over, the post-meeting statement has been shortened dramatically. Moreover, the press question-and-answer sessions have been cut to around half an hour from their customary 45 minutes or so.
Warsh said in October that the meeting schedule is another step in his plan to streamline communication. He indicated last month that the number of nonvoting meetings would increase to two in 2028.
"I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail," he said. "It's an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions. It's yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track."
The FOMC next meets Dec. 8-9. Its first meeting in 2027 will happen Jan. 26-27.
Correction: The Fed's October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates. The headline in an earlier version misstated the year.

China's increasingly assertive actions in the waters east of Taiwan threaten regional stability and freedom of navigation, G7 foreign ministers said in a joint declaration published late yesterday following a meeting ‌in Paris.
China, which claims Taiwan as its own, has stepped up activity off the nation’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols.
Officials in Taiwan say they believe China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.
While France, Germany, the UK and the US have all previously expressed their concern about China's actions off Taiwan's east coast, the G7 statement is the strongest unified expression of concern to date about the Chinese activities.
China's increasingly assertive activities in the waters east of Taiwan "threaten regional stability, freedom of navigation and the safety of international shipping," the statement said.
"We reaffirmed our opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo, particularly by force or coercion, or the threat thereof," it said.
The Chinese ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In Taipei, the Presidential Office welcomed the ‌G7 statement, saying peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait and the Indo-Pacific region are core issues vital to global security and prosperity.
Taiwan would continue working to strengthen its self-defense capabilities and cooperate closely with like-minded international partners, including G7 member states, Presidential Office spokeswoman Karen Kuo (郭雅慧) said in a statement.
Following the China Coast Guard's latest patrol off the east coast last month, Taiwan said China was harassing shipping and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction.
Taipei regards the area off its east coast as critical to wartime supply routes from allies in the event of a blockade or conflict. China's military operates around Taiwan on a daily basis.
China is carrying out "area denial" drills in the Western Pacific involving one of its aircraft carriers and other naval formations, Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said on Tuesday, following a reported rise in Chinese activities.
