The world's largest crypto fell 6% to $69,244.3 by 02:11 ET (07:11 GMT), falling below $70,000 for the first time since mid-August. It was also set to lose nearly 9% this week in its sixth straight week of losses.
Bitcoin extended a run of underperformance seen since October, pressured by a growing storm of headwinds for crypto markets.
Chief among these was the prospect of more interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, with markets growing increasingly convinced the central bank will raise rates as soon as December.
Markets were pricing in between 25 to 50 basis points of hike in December after consumer inflation data for October read hotter than expected, CME Fedwatch showed.
Higher rates tend to pressure speculative plays like crypto by limiting market liquidity and drawing more capital towards safer bets, like government debt.
Bitcoin has historically underperformed in high-rate environments.
Crypto markets were also hit by growing caution over the U.S. regulatory outlook, after the Democratic party won majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Strategy also emerged as a risk for Bitcoin this week, after MSCI said the world's biggest Bitcoin treasury, and others like it, will be excluded from its benchmark indexes effective November 30.
While the development does not present immediate selling risks for Bitcoin, it does limit Strategy's ability to raise new capital– which has been the firm's main source of funding for its massive Bitcoin purchases.
This could push Strategy into eventually selling more of its holdings– a move seen earlier this year– as it races to meet its mounting capital and debt obligations.

articles.title_orig: The downfall of Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: The downfall of Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
The US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between a Chinese businesswoman who had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing.
There is disagreement among US officials about the strength of the evidence that Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Chinese equivalent of the CIA, to spy on Jensen Huang — and, by extension, on US policymakers.
The FBI has been investigating Huang’s affair for at least a year. But Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that there are still “no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me, or by [FBI] Director Patel around who she is or is not.” President Donald Trump also hedged Thursday on whether the US had determined she was a spy, when commentator Stephen A. Smith asked whether Huang was right to have stepped down as CEO.
“Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” Trump said. “But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.”
Some officials at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, including those close to director Jay Clayton, have framed the characterization of Alice Huang as a Chinese spy as not entirely accurate and over-torqued, sources said. And officials at the CIA also are not yet convinced that the intelligence collection on Huang to date, including intercepted communications, proves she was knowingly funneling information back to Beijing, a source told CNN.
Still, some Trump officials told CNN that it strains credulity to believe that she was not acting as an agent of the Chinese government — simply by virtue of the fact that she is a successful Chinese businesswoman working with one of America’s most powerful companies .
Under Chinese national security law, Chinese citizens can be compelled to help gather intelligence on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party. Even if she had not done so yet, given her access to Huang — and by extension, to  Trump — some officials believe she posed a clear counterintelligence risk. But to others, the fixation on Huang’s relationship to the Chinese government has obscured broader questions around the US government’s failure to crack down on the diversion to China of sophisticated technology vital to the AI race.
Alice Huang’s Singapore-based company Megaspeed is a major purchaser of NVIDIA chips. The Department of Justice and the Commerce Department began an investigation into the firm in 2024 — part of a broader probe into an ecosystem of foreign shell companies suspected of diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China, a person briefed on the investigation said.
There are now questions brewing inside the White House over why the Commerce Department did not put Megaspeed on the so-called “entity list,” which restricts trade with companies that may pose a risk to US national security or foreign policy interests — at least while the investigation was ongoing, according to a person familiar.
“An intelligence operation wasn’t necessary to achieve that result,” a former Commerce Department official told CNN, noting that Jensen Huang has publicly advocated for the US to sell more chips to China. The fact that chips might be diverted to China through Megaspeed was, theoretically, a place where China’s interest already coincided with Nvidia’s — and “a regulatory loophole” already allowed it, the former Commerce official added.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Wednesday, following days of reports that he had had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Reports also emerged on Wednesday night that he separately had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia.
Democratic Rep. Jim Himes, the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, told POLITICO Thursday that he left a classified briefing with senior intelligence officials earlier this week unsure of the nature of Huang’s relationship with the Chinese government.
“What’s the relationship with Alice Huang and the Chinese, and what do we know about what influence or information was traded? Because today, at least, I don’t know,” Himes said.
Last year, when US intelligence officials first learned of the relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, officials across the government immediately wanted to know more — and some began sounding the alarm.
Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio warned in a memo in the spring about Jensen’s relationship with Huang, one source told CNN. But it is unclear how detailed the memo got on how much information Huang was or was not sharing with the Chinese government. Rubio briefed Trump on Jensen Huang and his relationship with Alice Huang aboard Air Force One en route to China in May.
The briefing occurred before Jensen Huang joined Trump in Alaska for the final leg of the trip, a source briefed on the matter told CNN.
Different agencies have continued conducting their own reviews of the intelligence, sources said. One particularly alarming development occurred when US intelligence  obtained communications that appeared to indicate someone with close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia was the source of information that ended up in Chinese intelligence streams, a person familiar with the investigation told CNN.
The FBI, which is conducting the primary counterintelligence investigation, told lawmakers last year that it was particularly suspicious of Alice Huang’s seemingly overnight career pivot from Chinese State television journalist to businesswoman with an unusually large amount of purchasing power in the Chinese economy, one of the sources said.
That, paired with her close relationship to the then-Nvidia CEO has continued to raise red flags inside the bureau, where the counterintelligence probe remains ongoing, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
Definitively linking suspicious behavior by Chinese nationals interacting with the United States to a state-directed spying campaign remains a perennial problem for counterintelligence officials trying to defend against Chinese espionage. It is notoriously difficult to collect intelligence on China, and China routinely compels its private citizens to do its bidding overseas.
When it comes to Chinese spying, the threat is in the eye of the beholder — some officials think the fears are overblown, other officials see a Chinese spy in every encounter.
“A lot of these people are guilty of just being Chinese,” said a former senior counterintelligence official.
But Joshua Hodges, a commissioner on the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, which investigates how US-China trade and economic ties affect American national security, said that “we’ve seen repeatedly the Chinese are incredibly adept at using people both wittingly and unwittingly.”
“Ultimately, what we typically see is those people, at a certain point in time, recognize that they know who they’re working for and they know the ends that they’re working towards,” he told CNN.
Hodges, who served on the National Security Council in Trump’s first term, noted Huang’s past rhetoric denouncing the phrase “China hawks” as “a badge of shame.”
“That clearly is directed to make people stop talking about the topic,” Hodges said. “You’ve got the biggest, one of the biggest, CEOs in the world attacking people for speaking out about something they care about — that clearly only benefits one country.”
CNN’s Kristen Holmes and Alejandra Jaramillo contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump Had Urged Nvidia’s Jensen Huang to Fight for His Job
articles.title_zh: Trump Had Urged Nvidia’s Jensen Huang to Fight for His Job
articles.content_orig:
President Trump called Jensen Huang on Tuesday, before the Nvidia chief stepped down amid a rapidly unfolding spy scandal, and urged him to keep fighting for his job, according to two people briefed on the conversation.
The call was the latest instance of Mr. Trump defending and protecting Mr. Huang, who had become a high-profile ally and an influential adviser on artificial intelligence. The president continued to back him to the end, even after U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Mr. Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
Nvidia announced on Thursday that Mr. Huang, who built the company into the world’s leading supplier of advanced A.I. chips, had been replaced as chief executive following revelations not just of the affair with the woman suspected of being a spy, but also another with one of his employees.
A representative for Mr. Huang did not provide a comment for this article. Neither Mr. Trump nor the White House responded to requests for comment about his call to Mr. Huang.
The president had been warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a Chinese citizen known as Alice Huang, whom intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.
Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”

articles.title_orig: Putin Had Four Plans to Defeat Ukraine. He Only Has Two Left.
articles.title_zh: Putin Had Four Plans to Defeat Ukraine. He Only Has Two Left.
articles.content_orig:
A woman looks out of a window of a damaged residential building in the Moscow region hit by what authorities described as a Ukrainian drone strike on Sept. 20. Stringer/Reuters
Amy Knight’s most recent book is The Kremlin’s Noose: Putin’s Bitter Feud With The Oligarch Who Made Him Ruler of Russia.
The new round of U.S.-mediated peace negotiations between Ukraine and Russia , scheduled to begin in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, is unlikely to make significant progress. Not only are Kyiv and Vladimir Putin ’s government far apart on key territorial issues and postwar security guarantees, but the Russian delegation is headed by Vladimir Medinsky, a firebrand Kremlin propagandist who has led past peace talks and made unacceptable demands. As Russian journalist Andrei Kolesnikov observed : “With Medinsky leading the delegation, the talks will go nowhere. His appointment as head of the delegation was already a signal from Putin: ‘Guys, our position isn’t changing.’”
Dangling the prospect of sanctions relief and business deals will not persuade Mr. Putin to reach a viable peace deal with Ukraine. He must instead face consequences that make continuing the war untenable for Russia.
Those consequences have already been mounting. A recent data leak from Rosstat, the Russian state statistics agency, revealed that 450,000 Russians have been killed since the war began. The country’s combat casualties are increasing so rapidly that recruitment of conscripts can no longer keep pace. Mr. Putin lacks the political capital for mass mobilization, so the regime has resorted to arresting men on flimsy charges and forcing them to sign military contracts. In the words of Russian commentator Maxim Katz, “the state is grinding through people at the front so quickly that its need for more will only grow and the methods of coercion will only become harsher.”
For all this horrific bloodletting, Russian forces actually lost around 27 square kilometres of territory on the battlefield in October. In addition, daily damage from Ukrainian strikes on factories, warehouses and refineries has cost billions of rubles. “If you look at the actual figures – the deaths, the destruction, the economic damage – then 2022, when we all lived in a state of constant horror, looks almost like a pre-war year from today’s perspective,” said Mr. Katz. “The death toll was a fraction of what it is now. Nobody was talking about oil refineries burning thousands of kilometres from the border.”
Russia pounds power facilities around Kyiv as temperatures plunge
The Kremlin is spending more than a trillion rubles a month on the war, and 17 trillion rubles have been allocated for defence in 2027. Although the Russian State Duma just approved the draft federal budget for 2027, which allows the government to collect an additional 1.5-trillion rubles in taxes from citizens and businesses next year, this will hardly be enough to prevent continued cuts in budgets for health care, education and business development.
Significantly, concerns about the budgetary shortfalls are now being expressed openly in the heavily censored Russian press. An editorial in Nezavisimaya Gazeta last month noted that, while the federal budget was meeting defence demands with tax hikes and tariffs, “mantras about the budget being sufficient to cover both defence needs and societal obligations serve only to defer any real reflection until the next budgetary cycle.”
The paper reported later that housing affordability in Russia was drastically declining: “Today, many Russians do not even have a room of their own. The deterioration of the housing stock and the number of dilapidated or unsafe residential buildings continue to grow.”
Meanwhile, high interest rates are preventing Russian companies from obtaining loans, while Western sanctions rule out raising capital from abroad. With the added challenges of rising costs, weakening domestic demand, higher taxes and shrinking profits, companies are freezing investment projects.
Russia, Ukraine exchange air strikes as U.S. envoy hails renewed security talks
Mr. Putin and his advisers doubtless realize that, with state resources stretched thin and the pool of potential combatants shrinking, sooner or later they will have to negotiate a peace settlement.
But ending the conflict without achieving all of Moscow’s declared aims has perils for Mr. Putin. As Russian political scientist Abbas Gallyamov recently pointed out , the huge casualties can be justified as a necessary price for gaining ultimate victory, but “if the war ends without a clear victory, an unavoidable question will arise: What did they die for?”
Mr. Putin needs to be persuaded that the negative consequences of continuing the war outweigh the risks of concluding it. That would require the U.S. to stand firmly with Ukraine’s European allies, making it clear to the Russian President that Washington and Europe will provide Ukraine with everything necessary to defeat Russia on the battlefield, defend itself against Russia’s drones and missiles, and continue to wreak havoc on Russia’s economy with air strikes against its energy and technological infrastructure. Faced with that prospect, Mr. Putin might be forced to conclude that he has no choice but to agree to a peace deal that is acceptable to Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Chabad Rov Faces Calls for Criminal Investigation Over Psak
articles.title_zh: Chabad Rov Faces Calls for Criminal Investigation Over Psak
articles.content_orig:
ב׳ כסלו ה׳תשפ״ז | November 12, 2026
An Israeli left-wing lawmaker called for a criminal investigation into Harav Gedalia Axelrod, following a psak he issued concerning the formation of an Israeli government supported by Arab political parties.
An Israeli lawmaker from the left-wing “Democrats” party has called for a criminal investigation into Harav Gedalia Axelrod , a senior Chabad rov and former Av Beis Din of Chaifa, following a halachic ruling he issued concerning the formation of an Israeli government supported by Arab political parties.
MK Michal Rozin called on Thursday for authorities to investigate Harav Axelrod, accusing him of incitement to violence and racism over a letter he published earlier this week.
In the letter, Harav Axelrod warned against establishing a government with the participation or support of Arab parties, ruling that political leaders who facilitate such a government fall under the halachic category one whose actions endanger the lives of others.
He further warned that lawmakers who allow such a government to be formed by abstaining from a vote would also bear responsibility for endangering Jewish lives.
Rozin responded on X, claiming that the rov’s statements crossed the line from religious expression into criminal incitement.
She drew comparisons to the period leading up to the 1995 assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzchak Rabin , warning that similar rhetoric directed at political leaders had preceded acts of violence.
The controversy comes amid statements by Democrats chairman Yair Golan , who has advocated forming a government with the participation of Arab parties. Golan has also called for ending what he describes as a “racist separation” between Jewish and Arab votes when determining which political bloc can form a government.
Following the publication of Harav Axelrod’s letter, the Center for Victims of Racism filed an urgent complaint with Israel Police, the Attorney General, and the State Attorney’s Office, demanding an investigation into possible offenses of incitement to violence, solicitation of murder, and incitement to racism.
The calls for criminal proceedings against the 85-year-old veteran rov drew criticism from the Israeli civil rights organization B’Tsalmo.
Its director, Shai Glick , accused left-wing politicians and organizations of attempting to silence rabbonim through the threat of criminal prosecution.
“The Knesset has barely begun, and the silencing has already started,” Glick said.
He called on prosecutors to dismiss the complaint, arguing that rabbonim and public figures should not face criminal prosecution merely for expressing their religious and halachic positions.
In response to the controversy, Chabad spokesman Rabbi Shimi Segal clarified that Harav Axelrod’s statements do not represent Chabad’s official position.
“Chabad’s official halachic positions are determined exclusively by the Chabad Rabbinical Court, in accordance with the Rebbe’s instructions,” he said. “Rabbi Axelrod is not a member of the court and does not hold a leadership position in Chabad. His statements and letters reflect his personal views alone.”
We appreciate your feedback. If you have any additional information to contribute to this article, it will be added below.
Does he really think Eizenkot has a din rodef and should be shot? If this is his halachic position then the government has no business mixing in and he shouldn’t be silenced by am horatzim for an opinion in a halachic matter. But I highly doubt that he meant that Eizenkot should actually be shot. So it is a case of bad wording and incitement which is criminal, especially if you are a rov with influence. So why shouldn’t he be made to at least retract?
I don’t know who you are, but I assume you are not a rov, and certainly not a dayan on a beis din. Rabbi Axelrod is. This is not the first time he has written a psak that others were afraid to write and publish. He knows what he is doing and understands the halachic reasoning behind what he wrote, and he ruled according to his Daas Torah that this is the halacha in this case. As a rov, paskening halacha is his job. All I expect from you is a little respect.
By the way, Chabad rabbonim wrote a similar psak about Rabin, and for obvious reasons, after he was killed, they erased the traces of it. You can read more in the book הרב אשכנזי.
the halacha states as one is a rodef even by mistake like a fetus someone who threatens to be moiser is also a rodef  even giving over monetary issues this all well known. about incitement, the left always incites calling people Nazi  and so on saying they are killing people in wars and so on, you don’t go against a brother and look at rules that are not kept  so much more by the left haters of israel the only question is are these statements useful probably not but at least we have a man with courage
After the catastrophe of Oslo, when שונאיהם של ישראל were being murdered in large numbers ר”ל and the Rabin government doubled down and invented the absurd phrase קורבנות השלום, some rabbonim declared that Mr Rabin had a דין רודף. The government went on to use the subsequent Rabin assassination as a pretext to quash much political opposition including especially many Rabbinical voices.

articles.title_orig: Finland detects strike on Russian warship as Zelenskyy meets US envoys
articles.title_zh: Finland detects strike on Russian warship as Zelenskyy meets US envoys
articles.content_orig:
Finland’s military says its forces have detected a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised mediation efforts led by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
A spokesperson for the Nordic country’s military said in an email to the Reuters news agency that its forces “detected … a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation”, adding that Finland is not under “any immediate military threat”.
The statement did not provide further details on where the strike originated, the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected.
Reuters said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused Wednesday’s strike.
Estonia shares a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea with Finland. Local media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship which had returned to Saint Petersburg after the alleged attack.
Ukraine’s Security Service has said it carried out the attack, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle. In recent days, Russia said it had intercepted at least 146 Ukrainian drones in the northwestern Leningrad region.
On Wednesday, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO warplanes were scrambled in response.
On Thursday, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ireland.
The US shuttle diplomacy followed trilateral negotiations in the United Arab Emirates this week, which produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners .
Russia’s state-run news agency TASS reported that the prisoner exchange should happen in two to three weeks. If finalised, it would be the latest in a long line of such exchanges.
“We are also working toward what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people with their families,” Kushner said on X on Thursday, following his meetings.

articles.title_orig: Four grizzly bears killed Canadian mother and daughter, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Four grizzly bears killed Canadian mother and daughter, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.
When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.
Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found . The search was now a tragic recovery effort.
The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 1.8 to 2.4 miles from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. On Nov. 11, the conservation service said forensic testing had confirmed that four bears — an adult female and her three offspring — captured in the traps were involved in the attack that killed Balcarras and her daughter.
"After considering the evidence and in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines, conservation officers dispatched all four bears to protect public safety," the agency said, adding that the investigation "found that the encounter likely involved predatory behavior."
"This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," Tyre said in the new statement.
The forensic testing also confirmed that the bears involved in the recent attack were not the same animals behind the attack on the school children last year.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said previously that the killings were triggering for the families traumatized by that attack.
"Our community is still healing," he said, adding that they've imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. "Our priority is to ensure they're safe and ensure our community is supported."
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear's behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.
Searchers found his niece's remains in a bear cache — a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
"Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult," he said.
By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
"There's no obvious body to identify," he said. "The coroner's investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs."
Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.
Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was "the central organizing person in our family," Matt Balcarras said.
"In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids," Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.
"She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies," he said. "She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They've lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades."
There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks . The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.
In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.
A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.
A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.
Ahmad  Mukhtar contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit
articles.title_zh: The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit
articles.content_orig:
Swedish activist criticised world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown
The planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”, said Greta Thunberg , who excoriated world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown in her first appearance at the annual UN climate talks in five years.
Thunberg , 23, the Swedish activist who became famous for heading the school climate strike movement, delivered her stark message to those gathered at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, amid the ongoing failure by countries to adequately address the climate crisis.
“It [Earth] is being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue,” Thunberg said.
“No one is coming to our rescue. When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights.”
Thunberg, who in recent years has shifted her focus towards other areas such as the conflict in Gaza , linked worsening global heating to other calamities such as war in an appearance alongside activists from Nepal, Canada and Australia.
“We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights and where basic necessities become luxuries,” she said.
“It’s more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be any less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.”
The intervention, on the fourth day of the two-week summit, came as world leaders who travelled to the Mediterranean coastal city delivered their own verdicts on the climate crisis and the faltering progress to address it.
Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, who was the only G7 leader to attend the talks, said in a speech that the record hot summer in the UK was “not normal”.
“The climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” said Burnham, who promised the UK would get to net zero emissions, and backed a proposal for countries to further electrify their economies.
Beth John, a climate justice adviser at Oxfam GB, said Burnham’s appearance “sends a positive signal”. But she added: “Showing up is not enough: a crisis of this scale needs substantive action, not just signals. The real test of climate leadership is delivery, not declarations.”
The electrification goal is one of the main potential promises expected at the talks, which are being jointly presided over by Turkey and Australia. Some countries want the agreement text to specify that the electricity will be derived from clean energy sources.
Campaigners have criticised governments for their slow pace of emissions cuts and for, so far, failing to rally around a phaseout of fossil fuels in the negotiations.
Current policies are set to heat the planet by 2.7C by the end of the century, a report by Climate Action Tracker found on Thursday. The catastrophic rise in temperatures is slightly more than the group expected last year and well above the 1.5C that world leaders have promised.
Thursday was rife with accounts of the harm caused by the climate crisis. Gita Chaudhary, Nepal’s environment minister, recounted the disastrous landslide – caused by a melting glacier – that struck the country in August, claiming more than 1,500 lives.
after newsletter promotion
“We call the catastrophic climate change event we suffered a mountain tsunami,” Chaudhary told the Guardian. “We lost people, we lost lives, we lost property. Nepal is working for rehabilitation, reconstruction and rebuilding the infrastructure. But the communities, the culture, the lives, we cannot revive.”
In the main conference room, a speech by Mohammad Mustafa, the prime minister of Palestine, drew a standing ovation from delegates as he described the environmental impact of the three-year war with Israel.
“Israel’s restrictions on access to land, water and natural resources have compounded Palestine’s climate challenges,” said Mustafa, who spelled out how widespread destruction in Gaza, including to water supplies, sewerage and farmland, had worsened environmental and health risks.
The Turkish hosts of Cop31 have repeatedly accused Israel of genocide and refused to invite the country’s leadership to Antalya. Israel denies that it has committed genocide and insists it has fought a legitimate war to safeguard its own security.
Another country not formally present at the talks is the US, which did not send a delegation. Donald Trump has withdrawn the country from the international climate framework, derided climate science as a “hoax”, and claimed he would not permit any new wind turbines.
This stance earned a rebuke from John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, who has made the trip to Turkey along with 20 Democratic members of Congress and two state governors. “He’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues,” Kerry said of Trump in response to a question from the Guardian.
The crushing midterm election win by the Democrats has raised hopes here at Cop of the US re-engaging on the climate crisis. But Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, warned the final two years of the Trump presidency would not see fundamental change on climate policy.
“I don’t want to romanticise what this will mean,” Newsom said on Thursday. “I don’t expect they’ll do anything but double down.”

articles.title_orig: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.title_zh: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.content_orig:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife
T he vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster .
The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.
The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.
It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.
Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.
Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.
“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.
“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”
Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.
“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.
More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.
Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.
Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.
Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.
after newsletter promotion
Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta , two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.
Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.
Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.
According to a Wall Street Journal report , the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.
In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on 30 October that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining.
In Oman , divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands.
But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said.
Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.”
Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems.
A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar – the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down – on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea.
Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface.
“Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades – so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

articles.title_orig: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then see Zelenskyy in Dublin
articles.title_zh: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then see Zelenskyy in Dublin
articles.content_orig:
The first direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in nearly a year ended on Wednesday without producing any breakthroughs. The US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi lasted two days, with both countries tentatively agreeing on a major prisoner exchange. However, there was no sign of progress on key issues including the Kremlin’s territorial demands and postwar security guarantees for Ukraine.
Ukrainian and Russian representatives both offered fairly upbeat assessments of the talks. Kremlin officials said the meetings had brought the prospect of a peace deal closer, while Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia commented that the renewed dialog provided “good momentum” and suggested that it may be possible to reach a solution by the end of the year.
At this stage, there is little evidence to support such optimistic assessments. On the contrary, the two sides appear to be as far apart as ever. Crucially, while Ukraine proposes using the current front lines of the war as the basis for a territorial settlement, Russia continues to demand that Ukraine also withdraw from the remaining 10 percent of the Donbas region that is still under Kyiv’s control.
Ukraine’s reluctance to retreat from the Donbas is grounded in harsh military realities. The territory that Russia insists on receiving before agreeing to a ceasefire includes a fortress belt of cities which is considered absolutely critical for Ukraine’s national defense. Handing this region over to the Kremlin without a fight would leave the rest of the country dangerously exposed and extremely vulnerable to further Russian advances. Nevertheless, Moscow refuses to moderate its position.
The Kremlin’s uncompromising approach to negotiations with Ukraine was summed up by Russian delegation head Vladimir Medinsky. “Every inch of Russian land will be returned to Russia, one way or another,” Medinsky commented on the sidelines of this week’s talks in the United Arab Emirates.
Medinsky’s rhetoric closely echoes Russian President Vladimir Putin’s own framing of the Ukraine invasion as a crusade to return what he frequently refers to as “ historically Russian lands .” In late October, Putin declared that Ukrainians have no right to the occupied regions of their own country. “I think it is not their territory, but the historical territory of Russia,” he comment ed .
Putin’s oft-stated insistence that Ukrainian land rightfully belongs to Russia leaves little room for any meaningful concessions and creates obvious obstacles to a lasting settlement capable of safeguarding the continued existence of an independent Ukraine. It also raises serious questions about the true extent of his territorial ambitions. While US officials have sought to focus peace talks on the Donbas issue , it seems self-evident that Putin has much bigger goals in mind.
Critics of a land-for-peace deal have argued that Putin seeks to seize the whole of Ukraine and sees the conquest of the Donbas region as a mere stepping stone toward this far grander objective. Many have noted that the Kremlin dictator’s historical claims are clearly not limited to eastern Ukraine’s Donbas. By his own twisted logic, Putin can hardly claim his place in Russian history if he captures the rust belt towns of the Donbas but leaves Kyiv, which he revers as “ the mother of all Russian cities ,” in enemy hands.
There are many red flags signaling Russia’s lack of interest in a genuine peace deal. For example, Putin’s vocal objections to the deployment of European troops in postwar Ukraine, along with his efforts to limit the size and capabilities of the Ukrainian military, do not suggest a man who is planning to live in peaceful coexistence with his Ukrainian neighbors. Instead, everything seems designed to create favorable conditions for the next stage of Russia’s invasion.
Likewise, regular Russian statements emphasizing the need to address the “root causes” of the war indicate aspirations that go far beyond the capture of the Donbas. While no definitive version of these root causes exists, the list of demands presented by Kremlin officials during previous bilateral talks reads like a playbook to undermine Ukrainian sovereignty and reestablish Russian dominance over the country. This has led many to conclude that as far as Vladimir Putin is concerned, the real root cause of the war is the existence of Ukraine.
These factors help to explain the lack of progress toward peace, but the brightest red flag of all is Putin’s claim that Ukrainian land is historically Russian. The Kremlin ruler’s Ukraine obsession reflects his conviction that the emergence of an independent Ukrainian state after 1991 was a grave injustice that left historical Russia divided. In order to reclaim his country’s great power status, Putin believes he must extinguish Ukrainian independence.
This belief is not Putin’s alone. Indeed, generations of Russian imperialists have struggled to suppress Ukraine’s statehood aspirations. Putin has now brought this toxic anti-Ukrainian ideology into the contemporary mainstream and made it a central pillar of modern Russia’s national discourse. His rants about returning historically Russian lands sound utterly unhinged to international audiences, but they are regarded as routine by the Russian public.
Anyone who wants to broker a peace deal with Vladimir Putin must first grasp the sheer scale of his imperial delusions. Putin believes he is on a sacred mission to revive the Russian Empire and will not be swayed by the promise of limited territorial gains or short-term economic incentives. Peace is still possible in such circumstances, but it must be peace through strength.
Peter Dickinson is editor of the Atlantic Council’s UkraineAlert service.
Russia’s bombardment of Ukraine’s civilian power grid qualifies as a crime against humanity, according to a new report by the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, writes Kateryna Odarchenko.
If Russia succeeds in overrunning an underfunded and exhausted Ukraine, the consequences for Europe will be catastrophic and the price tag of stopping an emboldened Putin will dwarf the current cost of supporting Kyiv, writes Peter Dickinson.
Russia’s recent setbacks in the Balkans are a reminder of the foreign policy challenges facing the Kremlin as the full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches a sixth year with no end in sight, writes Michael Getto.

articles.title_orig: Mercedes-Benz halts all further investment at German facilities
articles.title_zh: Mercedes-Benz halts all further investment at German facilities
articles.content_orig:
Mercedes-Benz announced on Thursday that it was halting all further investment at its German sites for the time being.
"The executive board has jointly decided to halt all further investments in German sites," Mercedes board member Michael Schiebe said in a memo on the company's intranet that was seen by the AFP news agency.
The company is also weighing plant closures , the memo added.
The announcement comes as the luxury German automaker faces increasing pressure from the works council and the IG Metall trade union.
Mercedes-Benz is "forced to examine, in concrete and detailed terms, which sites in Germany we can still afford to maintain," board of management member Britta Seeger said in an interview published on the company's intranet.
"We all want to avoid plant closures at all costs," she added. "Unfortunately, however, we must now pursue this option in more concrete terms."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Schiebe, the company's chief production officer, said the current cost structures meant it is not possible to invest in Germany.
German labor costs are sometimes five times higher than at plants in Eastern Europe, where administrative costs are also similarly much cheaper.
Schiebe had recently announced that two plants in Germany would have to close unless costs were reduced.
The carmaker , one of Germany's biggest and best-known brands, has been struggling with declining sales and profits in recent years.
Demand from China, the company's largest single market , which has historically accounted for around a third of Mercedes' passenger-car sales, has weakened considerably, particularly for luxury foreign brands. Mercedes' Chinese sales fell by around 19% in 2025.
The German carmaker has invested heavily in electric vehicles, but demand for EVs in Europe and in North America has been slower than many manufacturers anticipated. At the same time, Mercedes has also struggled with rising competition from cheaper EVs imported from China.

Increased US tariffs under President Donald Trump have also dented profits. Mercedes has said that tariffs alone cost it approximately €1 billion ($1.1 bln) in profit last year.
Several other leading German carmakers, including Volkswagen , BMW , Audi and Porsche, as well as other European manufacturers, have been facing similar problems.

The U.S. Air Force abruptly relocated more than a dozen aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England amid an emerging security threat, U.S. officials confirmed Tuesday.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the move, citing sources who said the threat originated in Iran.
As U.S. officials assessed the threat's nature and urgency, commanders raised the base's security level to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the military's second-highest alert level, indicating a likely terrorist threat against personnel or facilities.

U.S. Air Force KC-135, used for in-flight refueling, takes off from RAF Mildenhall Airbase. (AP Photo/Max Nash, File)
Flight-tracking data and open-source analysts with the Military Air Tracking Alliance identified 13 U.S. aircraft leaving the base late Monday, the Associated Press said.
Nine Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers were moved to airfields in Scotland, Germany and Spain.
Three CV-22B Ospreys were relocated to nearby RAF Lakenheath, which has hardened aircraft shelters.
A U.S. official told The Associated Press the moves were precautionary, noting that some aircraft were on rotational deployments while others were permanently stationed in the United Kingdom .

In early October, the Air Force pulled heavy bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after British counterterrorism police stopped three suspicious vans headed toward the base Sept. 27.
Two men have since been charged under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.
Separately, the Justice Department unsealed indictments against three Iranian-backed operatives on Tuesday accused of involvement in coordinated terrorist plots across Europe, including RAF Fairford.

articles.title_orig: Before His Ouster, Jensen Huang Belittled the Executive Replacing Him
articles.title_zh: Before His Ouster, Jensen Huang Belittled the Executive Replacing Him
articles.content_orig:
The most powerful woman in tech at this very moment is Colette Kress , the new interim CEO of Nvidia —but her predecessor, Jensen Huang , failed to mention her in a recent back-and-forth about the topic.
Earlier this fall, WIRED published a feature story exploring the complex topic of power for women working in an industry traditionally dominated by men. We questioned why Silicon Valley doesn't have an Elon-esque or Jensen-like female hero (or villain) and determined that the rubric of power still looks different for women, whether they manage to hold significant financial capital, flex their political prowess, dictate cultural norms, or run intellectual circles around the industry.
We also determined there wasn’t just one singular impressive woman in tech, but a whole lot of them: Lisa Su, Gwynne Shotwell, Laurene Powell Jobs, and dozens more. Kress, then-CFO of Nvidia, was also given a nod.
As part of the reporting process, WIRED wanted to include the insights of a few established men in Silicon Valley. So we emailed Huang directly to ask for his thoughts.
He responded that “[Meta’s] Dina Powell, [Google’s] Ruth Porat” came to mind, because he “see[s] them when I’m in DC.” After some prompting, Huang also agreed that Shotwell, the president and COO of SpaceX, was impressive.
Notably, Huang didn’t mention the highest-ranking woman executive in his own company, someone who joins him on nearly every quarterly earnings call and has deeper knowledge of Nvidia’s finances than probably anyone else in the world. As CFO, Kress was an integral part of one of the most valuable companies in the world—one of the most powerful women in tech by any measure.
As interim CEO, Kress now sits atop the bedrock of the entire AI industry at its most precarious moment. The choices she makes while in this role will reverberate across tech, geopolitics, and the broader economy.
Regardless of whether that promotion becomes permanent, we now know just how powerful Kress is in the tech industry—and that her omission from Huang’s list was just one in a long line of bad calls.

articles.title_orig: Home sales in worst slump since the aftermath of the Great Recession
articles.title_zh: Home sales in worst slump since the aftermath of the Great Recession
articles.content_orig:
Home sales fell to their lowest since 2010, a new report shows, in large part due to high mortgage rates. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.
Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.
"It was a punch in the gut," said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com . "We expected to see a soft month but not the softest month since 2010."
The drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.
In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023. Rates have gone down a bit since then, but are still well above where they were a year ago.
Higher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.
The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September to increase the cost of borrowing, including home mortgages. Fewer home sales and other purchases mean less economic activity, which the Fed wants in order to reach its goal of lowering inflation.
Policymakers at the Fed have signaled another rate hike could come in December, which could further slow down the housing market.
"It might seem like kicking the housing market while it's down right now for the Fed to continue a rate raising cycle but in the long run getting inflation under control is really the goal," Berner said.

articles.title_orig: Windward prices $175M IPO to advance China-licensed lung drugs
articles.title_zh: Windward prices $175M IPO to advance China-licensed lung drugs
articles.content_orig:
The Swiss biotech, which pocketed another $50 million through a concurrent private share sale to Sanofi, is developing a potential competitor to the blockbuster asthma treatment Tezspire.
Swiss immune drug developer Windward Bio on Thursday secured $175 million in its initial public offering, marking the biotechnology sector’s 30th so far this year.
The company, which formed just two years ago, met the projections it set earlier this week, selling about 10.3 million shares at $17 apiece. Windward starts trading on Friday under the ticker symbol “WWB.”
Sanofi, which had previously invested in Windward, purchased another $50 million in shares in a private stock sale. Prior to Windward’s IPO, the biotech had banked $365 million in venture funding.
Windward is testing a potential competitor to Tezspire, an asthma treatment that generated nearly $2 billion combined for its developers AstraZeneca and Amgen last year. Called WIN378, Windward’s top program is an “ ultra-long-acting ” injectable drug that, like Tezspire, targets an inflammatory protein known as TSLP. WIN378 is designed with certain enhancements that Windward believes might yield “ improved potency ” and less frequent dosing than Tezspire. Whereas AstraZeneca and Amgen’s blockbuster treatment is taken monthly, WIN378 could be dosed as little as twice a year, the company said in a regulatory filing.
The company is studying its lead drug in patients with severe, uncontrolled asthma and moderate-to-severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Interim data from the mid-stage portion of a Phase 2/3 trial in asthma showed that WIN378 was well-tolerated. It also helped trial participants expel more air while breathing out — a key measure of lung function — while lowering levels of a marker associated with airway inflammation. WIN378 also helped deplete counts of eosinophils, a type of white blood cell that can be overproduced when the immune system goes into overdrive.
Windward began the Phase 3 part of its asthma trial in September and anticipates reporting results next year. A mid-stage study in COPD, meanwhile, started in June and should produce data in 2027 as well.
The biotech is also developing a second treatment called WIN027, a bispecific antibody that targets TSLP and IL-13, another popular target for immune drugmakers. Windward said it expects Phase 1 findings from healthy trial participants in the first half of 2027. It recently launched two Phase 2b studies of WIN027 in people with COPD. A third trial in atopic dermatitis patients could also begin next year.
TSLP-targeting therapies are a crowded field, and Windward is competing with companies such as AbbVie , Pfizer , Upstream Bio and Generate Biomedicines . Some of those drug developers are working on multifaceted antibodies not unlike WIN027.
Both of Windward’s programs were licensed from Chinese drugmakers . WIN378 came from Kelun Biotech, which co-developed the treatment with Harbour BioMed. WIN027 was part of a deal with Qyuns Therapeutics . Windward paid $70 million up front in cash and equity to obtain those prospects, and is on the hook for another $1.6 billion in potential payments to those companies contingent on hitting certain R&D and sales milestones.
Windward chose to go ahead with its initial public stock sale as Rezera, the Boston biotech formerly known as NodThera, postponed its own offering “ due to market conditions ,” according to IPOScoop, a website tracking IPOs.
This year has been the busiest on record for drugmaker IPOs since 2021, with more than $8 billion raised among companies going public, according to BioPharma Dive data . Windward is also the ninth immune drug developer to price an IPO in 2026, a pace that now surpasses every year since 2018.

articles.title_orig: Howard Lutnick Took Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew
articles.title_zh: Howard Lutnick Took Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew
articles.content_orig:
Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology to Asia, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales in the region. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times
By Ana Swanson Tripp Mickle Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan
Ana Swanson, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported from Washington, and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang , was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company , sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

articles.title_orig: ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return
articles.title_zh: ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return
articles.content_orig:
Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation , according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.
An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.
One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.
Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset . The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.
Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.
It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned . In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.
One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.
Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”
Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

articles.title_orig: Turkey’s president calls the war in Gaza an ‘ecocide’ at the UN climate summit
articles.title_zh: Turkey’s president calls the war in Gaza an ‘ecocide’ at the UN climate summit
articles.content_orig:
Israel was not invited to the COP31 climate summit , which Turkey is hosting this year, Turkish Environment Minister and COP President Murat Kurum announced on Tuesday, citing Israel's actions in Gaza as the reason for its exclusion.
“As the host country for the leaders’ summit, we did not send an invitation to Israel,” Murat told Turkish media. “Of course, we will discuss the climate and climate justice here. We say that there can be no climate justice where peace does not prevail.”
The chairman of the Palestinian Environment Quality Authority, Zaghloul Samha, told The National that the decision was “a political issue, not a technical issue.”
The exclusion comes as climate negotiations involving nearly 200 countries seek agreement on a Turkish proposal to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels . However, statements by world leaders at the summit have increasingly focused on geopolitical conflicts and Israel's role in the region, raising questions about whether climate discussions are being overshadowed by political disputes.
"A year ago, the planet left COP30 invigorated... [but] this momentum has dropped off at the start of this year. Climate change disappeared from the speeches and documents from global leadership," Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, whose country hosted last year's conference, told the summit. "We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations. The planet cannot be at the mercy of hegemonic struggles."
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told world leaders earlier in the day that the international community's slow response to climate change had put the world on a path to destruction and that urgent action was needed to avert the worst consequences. A UN report last month found that the world was on course to exceed the 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan also used the summit to criticize Israel over the humanitarian situation in Gaza , accusing it of preventing the delivery of containers to Palestinians displaced by the conflict.
“Today, we are asking Israel for containers. But right now, our Palestinian brothers and sisters in Gaza are unfortunately being forced to live in tents surrounded by mud,” he said, addressing recent rains that have flooded tents housing displaced Palestinians. “Are these people not human? Are they not even considered deserving of a tent? We want to send containers, but we are not being given permission to do so.”
The IDF confirmed earlier this week that 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks carrying winter supplies have entered Gaza, following criticism from Hamas over weather conditions damaging tents.
Greenpeace Israel used the occasion to criticize the government over its fossil fuel policies, accusing it of “opening the Mediterranean Sea to more gas companies and continuing to endanger the environment and climate targets.”
The environmental organization was responding to an announcement by the Energy Ministry on Monday that American oil and gas company Murphy Oil would join gas exploration efforts in the Mediterranean after Israel granted the company and Israeli firm Ratio six new licenses.
“Although Israel is absent from the conference, the decisions made there will also affect our future. The conference is a key tool in the global effort to tackle the climate crisis, with governments making decisions on reducing emissions and financing preparations for the impacts of the crisis,” the organization said. “In a year in which the war with Iran, alongside geopolitical tensions, has exposed the risks associated with oil and gas, and even led to ‘fossil fuel inflation,’ the climate conference offers renewed hope for change.
“At stake are accelerating the transition from fossil fuels, the biggest driver of the climate crisis, to renewable energy; protecting communities that contribute the least to the crisis but suffer its consequences the most; and halting the destruction of forests."
While Israel was not invited to the conference, and the US was not in attendance, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was present and used the summit to raise Tehran's grievances against Israel and the United States, according to an announcement by the Iranian government on Wednesday.
"In these meetings, we will discuss the legitimate positions of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the crimes committed by the United States and Israel in the region, as well as how they have witnessed the consequences of their heinous actions in elections in their own countries, at the hands of their own people," Pezeshkian said. "Not only in the United States and Israel, but also in Europe, the results of the elections that have taken place have all been contrary to the wishes of warmongers, aggressors and those who falsely speak of democracy and human rights while acting against all these principles.”
